title: Warp-level utilization audit and quick experiments
content:
Purpose:
Quick, pragmatic audit of warp-level utilization and occupancy behavior observed in recent Nsight runs for sequence-length 2048 transformer workloads. This doc captures raw observations from profiling sessions, targeted micro-experiments, and short hypotheses for follow-ups. Aim is to produce 1–2 actionable changes we can test on a Canary Dedicated node this week.

Context / why this matters:
- Several production p99 latency spikes traced to GPU-side stalls on long-sequence paths (SR-4871).
- Nsight timelines show low SM-level compute utilization despite high memory bandwidth and many small kernel launches.
- We need to know whether the issue is: (a) kernel launch overhead (many tiny kernels), (b) poor warp execution efficiency (control divergence), or (c) memory-bound kernels hitting serialization (atomic contention / scatter-heavy ops).

Test rig (hardware & software):
- GPU: NVIDIA A100 80GB (PCIe) and one run on H100 to sanity-check kernel behaviour.
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.3, cuBLAS/cuDNN stacks from our pinned infra image (image: redwood-inference/gpu-runtime:2025-04-28).
- Model: trimmed Llama-2 style 7B float16 with KV cache ~ 2048 tokens during generation.
- Serving runtime: branch perf/warp-audit (see PR 786) with hooks to toggle CUDA Graph capture and persistent-thread blocks.
- Tools: Nsight Systems (nsys 23.11), Nsight Compute (ncu 23.11), `nvprof` not used (deprecated).

Commands used (representative):
- nsys profile --capture-range cudaProfilerApi --output nsight_session_2025-05-03 \
  --trace=cuda,cudnn --stats=true --sample=none --force-overwrite -- \n  /opt/redwood/bin/serve --config perf/seq2048.yaml
- ncu --target-processes all --set full --save yes --export nvprof nsight_ncu_2025-05-03
- small kernels microbench: ./microbench/kernel-launch-overhead --iters 10000 --block-size 128

High-level observations from Nsight timeline:
- Pattern A (dominant): Burst of many small kernels (~500–1500 kernels) per token step, each ~2–12us. Between bursts there are gaps where SMs idle waiting on CPU work (launch overhead).
- Pattern B (occasionally): A few large compute kernels (~100–300us) with high DRAM throughput but low achieved occupancy (~30–45%).
- CUDA Graph capture reduces CPU-side gaps significantly — wall-clock per-token drops ~18% in baseline tests — but SM-level achieved occupancy for the big kernels did not change much.
- Warp execution efficiency metric in NCU often sits 62–78% on the large kernels, implying divergence or masked lanes in some pathways.

Detailed NCU metrics (representative sample):
- kernel: multi_head_attn_fwd
  - duration: 210us
  - achieved_occupancy: 0.37
  - warp_execution_efficiency: 0.71
  - l2_read_throughput: 480 GB/s
  - dram_read_throughput: 220 GB/s
  - instructions_per_cycle (SM): 0.42
- kernel: rotary_pos_enc_apply (small)
  - duration: 8us
  - launch_overhead_effective_fraction: high (many launches)

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Launch-heavy micro-kernel fanout: The runtime emits many small elementwise kernels per token due to per-layer callback chains (locking/trace hooks). This incurs CPU->GPU latency and prevents continuous SM occupancy.
2) Block/warp sizing mismatch for attention matmul variants: Certain GEMM kernels are launching with small blocks because of padding/sequence remainder logic, leading to low achieved occupancy.
3) Divergence in fused kernels for rotary/attention masking: Conditional masks cause warps to execute masked lanes inefficiently.
4) L2/DRAM contention from concurrent memcpy/IO streams (NVLink transfers or host->device prefetch) creating stalls that manifest as low IPC even during high bandwidth.

Short experiments run and outcomes:
- Experiment 1: Enable CUDA Graph capture for entire token loop (capture per-request)
  - Result: Token p50 reduced ~10–18%, CPU visible gaps mostly eliminated. Nsight timeline shows fewer launches but big kernels unchanged in occupancy.
  - Notes: Graph works but fragile for dynamic-length sequences; we need a safe fallback path.

- Experiment 2: Increase blockDim.x for small elementwise kernels (from 128 to 256) in microbench
  - Result: Small kernels per-launch duration reduced 20–35% and total per-token launch count reduced (merged threads per launch). Good for launch overhead but not addressing large-kernel occupancy.

- Experiment 3: Force fused attention path to use cublasLt with larger tile sizes (when available)
  - Result: Some GEMM kernels dropped from 210us -> 150us and occupancy improved to ~0.52 in that path on H100, but on A100 the implicit tiling by cuBLAS still left remainders that reduced occupancy.

- Experiment 4: Turn off host-side tracing hooks (temp) and reprofile
  - Result: CPU->GPU gaps further reduced; small but measurable improvement in warp efficiency (up to +3%). Indicates tracing callbacks were contributing to jitter.

Actionable short-term changes (can be applied to Canary Dedicated):
1) Default-enable token-loop CUDA Graph capture behind a feature flag (perf.cuda_graphs=true) and add guard rails for dynamic lengths (fallback after X growth in length). Target milestone: canary rollout by 2025-05-14.
2) Add a micro-optimization to merge small elementwise kernels in the runtime: batch per-layer elementwise ops into a single invocation when safe. Implementation WIP in PR 786; test matrix: seq 256/1024/2048.
3) Add a scheduling heuristic: avoid launching small kernels during the steady-state token loop when a large GEMM is queued — coalesce them on host side to reduce inter-kernel gaps. Low-risk config toggle in serving config.

Medium-term investigations (next sprint):
- Investigate codegen changes to improve occupancy for the big matmul kernels: tweak thread-block sizes and shared-memory tiling to reduce remainder-waste (ticket: PERF-4927).
- Deeper dive into warp divergence sources using NCU's Source View and `warp_scheduling_efficiency` counters to find branches on per-token masks. May need to refactor masking to use predicated/vectorized ops.
- Explore persistent-kernel patterns (single persistent thread block handling multiple token steps) vs CUDA Graph for long-lived contexts. Both reduce launch overhead but have different memory/access tradeoffs.
- Run controlled NVLink/DRAM contention tests by isolating copy streams to see if concurrent host->device copies reduce IPC/occupancy.

Open questions / risks:
- CUDA Graph capture helped a lot for launch overhead, but it makes hot-patching (patching token-level callbacks for evals/observability) harder. How much observability do we accept to win latency?
- Some changes (cublasLt tiling, block-size tweaks) show divergent behaviour across A100/H100; need fleet-wide profiling before enabling by default.
- Persistent kernels increase complexity for multi-tenant workloads where we rely on preemption. Is that acceptable for Dedicated? Probably yes, but needs SRE ops guidance.

Immediate next steps (this week):
- Diego: put together a safe CUDA-graph capture experiment in Canary config and run 12h stability test (linked: SR-4871).
- Priya: finish microkernel merge prototype in PR-786 and run regen perf matrix for seq 256/1024/2048.
- Ava (me): schedule deep NCU run with Source View and collect warp_scheduling_efficiency for the top 10 longest kernels. Also post summary to #perf-gpu and update CONFLUENCE-4521.

Appendix / raw snippets:
- nsight capture excerpt (timeline notes):
  - 00:01:12.345 -> 00:01:12.560: multi_head_attn_fwd (210us) x 48
  - 00:01:12.561 -> 00:01:12.569: rotary_pos_enc_apply (8us) x 128
  - recurring gap of ~15–30us between bursts (CPU scheduling/launch)

- Quick microbench result table (avg over 10 runs):
  - baseline small-kernel count per token: 620, total small-kernel time: 5.1ms
  - merged-kernel count: 120, total small-kernel time: 3.2ms
  - per-token latency reduction (merged kernels only): ~14%

- Links/refs: PR 786, ticket PERF-4927, CONFLUENCE-4521 (notes + raw NCU exports), slack #perf-gpu thread 2025-05-05 (contains nsys trace zip)
